summary: Bahrain is an island kingdom in the Persian Gulf, in ancient times the center of the Dilmun civilization, known for its history of pearl diving, and in 1932 it became one of the first countries in the Gulf to discover oil.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Bahrain accepted Islam in the 7th century while the Prophet Muhammad was still alive (around 628). Shia make up the majority of Bahraini citizens, who are descendants of the ancient local Baharna people; in 1783 the Sunni Al Khalifa family came in from Qatar and took over Bahrain, creating a situation of Sunni royal rule over a Shia majority, to which the protest movement of 2011 was also related. Because foreign residents make up about half, Muslims make up about seven tenths of the whole population.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christians are mostly foreign workers from India, the Philippines and Western countries. Bahrain is a Gulf country with relatively open religious attitudes: in the early 20th century American Reformed missionaries opened the American Mission Hospital, in 2021 Bahrain completed the Our Lady of Arabia Cathedral, the largest Catholic cathedral in the Persian Gulf, and in 2022 Pope Francis also visited Bahrain.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly migrant workers and merchants from India. Indian merchants were already running pearl and spice trade in Bahrain in the 19th century, and the Shreenathji Temple in Manama is said to be about 200 years old, one of the oldest Hindu temples in the Gulf. After oil extraction began in the 1930s, the number of Indian immigrants rose greatly.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhists are mainly foreign workers from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Nepal and other countries, mostly working in services and as domestic helpers. They meet mainly in private venues, and because most are short-term contract workers, the Buddhist community accounts for about 3 percent of the total population.

religion.background: Ancient Bahrain was the center of the Dilmun civilization and from the 3rd millennium BCE was a trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. Before Islam arrived in the 7th century, the island had Nestorian Christian and Zoroastrian communities. Bahrain has a long Shia tradition, and since the Sunni Al Khalifa family took power in 1783, the difference in sect between the royal family and the majority of the population still affects politics today. After oil extraction in the 20th century, large numbers of foreign workers brought religious diversity, and Bahrain is also known for its relatively tolerant policy of allowing churches and temples to be built.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is Bahrain's official language and the mother tongue of its citizens; the local spoken forms include the Baharna dialect of the Shia Baharna residents and a dialect close to Gulf Arabic spoken by the Sunni residents. Because foreign residents make up about half, about half the population speak Arabic as a mother tongue, and the government, courts and schools use Modern Standard Arabic.

ranking.name: Malayalam
ranking.description: Malayalam is the language of the Indian state of Kerala; Keralites began going to work in Bahrain after oil was discovered there in the 1930s, and immigration increased greatly after oil prices rose in the 1970s. They mostly work in construction, commerce, medicine and education, forming one of Bahrain's largest immigrant language communities.

ranking.name: Urdu
ranking.description: Urdu speakers are mainly Pakistani immigrants, and there are also many Pakistanis in the Bahraini police and security forces, a tradition that goes back to the practice of recruiting South Asian personnel as guards during the British protection period. Urdu is mutually intelligible with Hindi and is widely used among South Asian migrant workers.

language.history: Since Islamization Bahrain has used Arabic, and the dialect of the Shia Baharna retains older features and has been influenced by Persian and Aramaic. From 1820 Britain signed treaties with the Bahraini rulers, and from 1861 Bahrain became a British protectorate, and English began to appear in administration and commerce. In 1932 Bahrain was the first on the Arab side of the Persian Gulf to discover oil, attracting large numbers of workers from India, Iran and other countries. After independence in 1971 Arabic is the official language, while English is used in commerce, education and among foreign communities.

ranking.name: Machboos
ranking.description: Chicken, lamb or fish is stewed together with long-grain rice, with dried lime, saffron, cinnamon and baharat spice added, so that the rice is richly fragrant.
ranking.history: Machboos is regarded as Bahrain's national dish; the rice and spices were formerly all imported from India and Persia through Indian Ocean trade, reflecting Bahrain's history as a trading hub of the Persian Gulf. Before the oil era Bahrain was an important pearl-diving center, and fishermen and pearl divers often made machboos with fish. Today it is the most common main dish at family meals, weddings and the breaking of the fast during Ramadan.

ranking.name: Muhammar
ranking.description: Fish such as safi (rabbitfish) is grilled or fried and served with sweet rice cooked with date syrup or sugar and saffron and cardamom, blending sweet and savory.
ranking.history: Muhammar means 'reddened', referring to the reddish-brown color the rice takes from the date syrup. The date palm is the most important crop of the island of Bahrain, and in the past the island's oases had large date groves. It is a traditional dish particular to Bahrain, closely connected to the lives of local fishermen and pearl divers, and often appears at family meals and festivals, eaten with grilled or fried fish.

ranking.name: Harees
ranking.description: Wheat grains are stewed with chicken or lamb for a long time and then repeatedly beaten into a sticky porridge, served with ghee poured over and sprinkled with cinnamon; the texture is smooth and the taste mild.
ranking.history: Harees is one of the oldest dishes of the Arabian Peninsula and is recorded in Arabic cookbooks of the 10th century. In Bahrain it is a traditional dish for breaking the fast in Ramadan and for Eid al-Fitr, and neighbors often share it with one another. The Shia community also prepares large pots of harees during Ashura and gives it to those who come to take part in the commemoration, symbolizing the spirit of sharing and charity.

ranking.name: Bahraini Halwa
ranking.description: A translucent, jelly-like sweet cooked from cornstarch, sugar, saffron, rose water and cardamom, with nuts added; the texture is soft and chewy.
ranking.history: Bahraini halwa is Bahrain's most representative sweet, and the family workshops near Manama are the most famous, among them old-established shops such as 'Showaiter' that have been passed down through several generations. Making it requires stirring for a long time in a large pot and is very physically demanding. It is the sweet that Bahrainis serve to guests with Arabic coffee, and it is also often given as a gift to relatives and friends.

ranking.name: Balaleet
ranking.description: Thin vermicelli noodles are stir-fried with sugar, saffron, rose water and cardamom and topped with a layer of fried egg, blending sweet and savory; it is a traditional breakfast.
ranking.history: Balaleet is a traditional breakfast of the Gulf region, eaten especially on the mornings of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. The combination of vermicelli, saffron and rose water reflects the trade between the Gulf and Persia and India. In the past sugar and spices were expensive and were used only at festivals; today it is an everyday breakfast option in Bahraini homes and traditional restaurants.
